questions.stem_html:
A 34-year-old aid worker returns from West Africa and develops fever, confusion, jaundice, and oliguria. Thin blood smear shows delicate ring forms, sometimes more than one in a single erythrocyte, and crescent-shaped gametocytes. Parasitemia is 8%. Brain imaging shows no focal lesion. The patient is treated urgently for severe malaria.

Which parasite property most directly contributes to his neurologic dysfunction?

options.text_html: Antigenic variation of a flagellar surface protein in the bloodstream
Expression of PfEMP1 on infected erythrocytes, causing endothelial adhesion and microvascular sequestration
Granulomatous inflammation around parasite eggs in cerebral venules

questions.explanation_html: Falciparum-infected erythrocytes display variant surface proteins such as PfEMP1 that bind endothelial receptors. Sequestration and rosetting obstruct small vessels and contribute to cerebral malaria and organ failure. PfEMP1-mediated cytoadherence prevents splenic clearance and concentrates infected cells in the microcirculation, impairing tissue perfusion.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Hypnozoites occur with P vivax and P ovale and cause relapse, not falciparum cerebral sequestration.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: P vivax preferentially infects reticulocytes; falciparum can invade erythrocytes of all ages and achieve high parasitemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Plasmodium blood stages do not use a flagellar antigen to cause cerebral malaria.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Egg-induced granulomas are characteristic of helminth infections, not malaria.

questions.educational_objective: Explain severe falciparum malaria through infected-erythrocyte cytoadherence, rosetting, and microvascular sequestration rather than hypnozoite relapse.
